summary: Asked to pass a message to the Instagram group from Signal, Nora said she couldn't — while listing Instagram as one of the places she can send to. She can; the instructions for that tool misled her twice.
details: Asked to 'go to the IG group and ask', she replied that none of the places she can reach is an 'IG group'. The instructions gave her four exact words and described the target as a room, so she looked for a room with that name instead of recognising IG as Instagram. It now says plainly that the thing being named is a network, that people will call it whatever they call it, and that her job is to work out which one they mean.

She also said she would not ask people using someone's name. The instructions had meant to reassure her — a passed-on message arrives marked as coming from whoever asked, so she is not pretending to be them — and she read it as a rule forbidding her from using their name at all. Reworded so it reads as the reassurance it was: passing something on is not speaking for someone, and it is the point of the tool rather than a reason to avoid it.

Nothing about how messages are passed on changed. The wiring was already correct and was verified separately: from the Signal group it resolves to the right Instagram group, and the permission check passes. She simply never reached for the tool.
limitations: This changes what she is told, not what she can do, so how reliably she now reaches for the tool is a judgement call by a model and has not been measured across many phrasings.
She can still decline to pass a particular message on. That is deliberate — the rewording separates 'I won't carry this' from 'I'm not allowed to', and only the second was wrong.
Still one room per network per group. Asking for a specific room by name, where a group has more than one on the same network, is not something this can do.
